transcript.text: Is it normal for my dishwasher to leave everything wet? Plastic tubs are soaking every time and there's drips on the glasses. It's a Bosch Serie 4.

Some wetness is normal, particularly for plastic tubs: plastic does not retain enough heat to evaporate water, so it often comes out wetter than glass or china. A few droplets on glasses can also be normal with condensation drying, especially after an Eco or short programme. If everything is genuinely wet, the usual causes are rinse aid being low or set too low, using an Eco/Quick cycle, or items being positioned so they hold pools of water. A heater fault is mainly a possibility if the whole wash is cold as well. 1. Check and top up the rinse-aid dispenser, then increase its setting one step if it is already full. Rinse aid helps water sheet off rather than remain as droplets.
2. For the next load, use a full Normal/Intensive programme rather than Eco or Quick, and avoid nesting cups and tubs. Leave the door slightly ajar when the cycle finishes if your machine has not opened it itself.
3. The key check: at the end of a cycle, are the dishes hot/warm or cold—and is there rinse aid in the dispenser? Hot but wet points to drying settings/normal condensation behaviour; cold dishes would point towards a heating problem.

Thanks. The dishes are hot and steamy inside at the end, so it's heating fine. The rinse aid symbol is lit though, so it's empty. I use all-in-one tablets. I always run Eco 50 and open the door straight away when it finishes.

This does not sound like a heater fault: hot, steamy dishes show it is heating. The lit rinse-aid symbol is the most likely reason for the droplets on the glasses, and Eco drying plus plastic tubs explains much of the rest. All-in-one tablets can contain a little rinse-aid substitute, but they often do not give the same drying result as liquid rinse aid, especially on Eco. 1. Keep using Eco if you prefer it, but expect plastics to remain wetter than china or glass. Tip tubs/cups so they cannot collect a pool of water.
2. Opening the door at the end is helpful; leave it ajar for a few minutes rather than closing it again straight away.
3. Judge the result after one or two washes with rinse aid topped up. Glasses should be noticeably drier; some moisture on plastic is normal. If glasses and crockery are still soaking wet after that, try one Normal/Intensive cycle as a comparison. If they dry properly on that programme, it is simply the Eco drying performance rather than a fault.
Ok, I'll top up the rinse aid and try it. Do I still need the rinse aid if I use all-in-one tablets? And should I try a different programme if it's still wet?

Yes — use liquid rinse aid even with all-in-one tablets, particularly if the rinse-aid light is on and you want better drying. The tablet’s rinse-aid substitute is often not enough on an Eco cycle. Fill the dispenser and, if the result is still droplet-heavy after a wash or two, increase the rinse-aid setting by one step. If it is still wet afterwards, try one full Normal/Intensive programme as a comparison rather than changing tablets straight away. If glass and crockery dry much better on that programme, the dishwasher is behaving normally: Eco drying is gentler, and plastic tubs will still usually retain some water. If glasses and china remain very wet even with rinse aid and on the hotter/full programme, that would justify looking further at drying settings or the appliance. The heating side is unlikely here because the dishes are hot and steamy at the end.

candidates: Rinse aid level or dose / normal condensation drying (high)
Eco or quick programme with limited drying (medium)
